newsitem.title: USA: Treasury changes financing mix to lure investors.
newsitem.headline: Treasury changes financing mix to lure investors.

text.p: The Treasury's decision to scrap some bond sales and broaden its menu of inflation-indexed securities is mainly a sales tactic to lure more foreign and domestic buyers, analysts said Tuesday.

The Treasury Department said Monday it was dropping two sales of fixed-rate 10-year notes in July and October -- cutting sales to four times a year from six -- partly because a shrinking budget deficit requires less borrowing.

The Treasury also said it would offer more inflation-protected notes to include a five-year maturity for auction in July and October. A new 10-year indexed note will be unveiled in January and inflation-indexed 30-year bonds and U.S. Savings Bonds will be sold later next year.

Six years of economic growth and a booming stock market have given the Treasury exceptional leeway to rejig its array of debt offerings. With tax revenues pouring into government coffers, the department has more, potentially cheaper, choices on ways to finance the budget deficit, the annual shortfall between government spending and income.
"This is just the right time to experiment with these things," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis. "Treasury is not really under the gun, so they've got many more options."
Indexed bonds, whose returns vary based on changes in the government's Consumer Price Index, are a less expensive way for the federal government to borrow when inflation is stable as it is now.
A lower "inflation premium" can be offered on these securities than on conventional bonds or notes because there is a mechanism to keep returns from being eaten away by inflation.
Other countries, including Britain, Sweden and Canada, recognised the benefits of inflation-indexed bonds years ago, so the Treasury's move into that arena is somewhat belated.
Sohn said foreigners bought about three-fourths of all U.S. debt issued last year so it made sense to offer them a security they are familiar with and that also offers some inflation protection.
It is basically a matter of appealing to more tastes.

"It's no different from selling a car -- you want a small car, a big car, a red car and a blue car to get the buyers in," Sohn said, adding inflation-protected securities should meet some investors' needs while offering modest savings for the government.

"We expect, on the basis of logic and international experience, that we'll over time reduce the government's funding costs,' Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said. The first 10-year indexed notes, sold in January and in April, met with a good response.
"A liquid market has developed," Summers said, though only about $15 billion of the indexed securities have been sold.
Inflation-protected debt is unlikely to become a major factor in government debt management for a long time, considering more than $5 trillion of debt is outstanding.

"They're primarily oriented at long-term savers and retirement accounts," said economist Richard Berner of Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh, so they tend to be bought and then tucked away into those accounts.
That tends to limit their appeal. Since they do not trade as often as regular bonds, the market for them is less liquid.

Indexed securities also can help portfolio managers reduce the risk from inflation when balancing holdings of stocks, bonds and cash. That makes them "a useful addition to the pantheon of fixed-income securities," Berner said.

Remarkable progress in shrinking the budget deficit made it easier to bring indexed securities to market, but raised concern among traders about a shrinking flow of government debt issues that are the benchmark for most other lending.
The deficit peaked at $290.4 billion in the year ended Sept. 30, 1992. This year it is expected to be under $100 billion.
One big benefit from the lower deficit is that more money can be put into other, more productive investments than government bonds, officials said.

Still, bond investors should not fret about supply, Summers said. "We're certainly not getting to the point of worrying that we won't be able to offer enough bonds to keep the government bond market liquid," he said.
